units.title: Unit 93 — Expressions with come and go
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 93. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the major senses and complements of come and go phrasal verbs.
Use common come to and come into collocations with natural prepositions and nouns.
Recognise fixed go expressions and choose meanings from context.

sectionsChecked: A: Phrasal verbs based on come
B: Collocations with come to and come into
C: Phrasal verbs based on go
D: Other expressions based on go

items.example: The outdoor concert never came off because of the storm.
items.note: In this sense, come off means that a planned event actually happens, often in questions or negatives.

items.example: The exam results will come out on Friday.
items.note: Results, reports or information can come out when they become public.

items.example: Several unexpected questions came up during the interview.
items.note: A topic or problem comes up when it is mentioned or arises.

items.pt: passar na casa de alguém; fazer uma visita informal
items.example: Why don't you come round for coffee next weekend?
items.note: Mainly British English in this sense; American English often uses come over or come around.

items.example: He refused to let a disagreement come between him and his brother.
items.note: Come between two people or priorities means damage their connection or create a barrier.

items.example: I came across an interesting article while browsing an archive.
items.note: Usually refers to an unexpected discovery, not a planned search.

items.example: How did you come by such a rare first edition?
items.note: Often suggests acquiring something in an unusual or uncertain way.

items.example: The price of second-hand laptops has come down this year.
items.note: Here the subject is a price, cost or amount; no direct object is needed.

items.pt: ter uma ideia; propor uma solução
items.example: Our team came up with a practical solution to the delay.
items.note: Come up with an idea, suggestion or solution; the object follows with.

items.example: After several meetings, both companies came to an agreement.
items.note: Typical partners include parties, negotiators and groups; agreement is countable here.

items.example: After reviewing the data, we came to a different conclusion.
items.note: Means reach a judgement after considering evidence.

items.pt: tomar uma decisão; chegar a uma decisão
items.example: We need to come to a decision before the deadline.
items.note: Decision is singular with a; compare make a decision.

items.example: It took her months to come to terms with the unexpected result.
items.note: Means learn to accept a difficult fact emotionally, not just understand it.

items.example: Traffic came to a standstill after the bridge was closed.
items.note: Used for traffic, movement, work or an activity that stops entirely.

items.example: The long negotiations finally came to an end.
items.note: Neutral expression for something finishing; often uses finally.

items.example: Several researchers came into contact with unfamiliar materials.
items.note: Used for meeting people or making physical contact with a substance.

items.example: She came into a fortune when her aunt died.
items.note: Usually means inherit a large amount of money.

items.example: The organisation came into existence in the early 1990s.
items.note: Describes the beginning of the existence of something.

items.example: Brightly coloured jackets have come into fashion again.
items.note: For styles or trends becoming popular.

items.pt: entrar em funcionamento; começar a operar
items.example: The new control system will come into operation next month.
items.note: Used for machines, rules, systems or procedures starting to function.

items.example: The lighthouse came into sight as the boat approached the coast.
items.note: Describes something becoming visible, often while you are moving.

items.example: A small village came into view beyond the hills.
items.note: Similar to come into sight; it emphasises becoming visible.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go on
items.example: There's a lot of noise outside; what's going on?
items.note: Use What is going on? to ask what is happening.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go on
items.example: She went on studying even when the library was closing.
items.note: Go on doing something means continue doing the same activity.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go on
items.example: As the evening went on, the discussion became more relaxed.
items.note: Time goes on as it passes.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go on
items.example: You go on ahead; I'll join you after this call.
items.note: Used when one person leaves or proceeds before another.

items.pt: reclamar repetidamente com; pegar no pé de
items.section: C · Different meanings of go on
items.example: My flatmate keeps going on at me about the dishes.
items.note: Mainly British informal use: go on at someone about something.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go through
items.example: They went through a difficult period after the closure.
items.note: To endure or experience something, usually unpleasant.

items.section: C · Different meanings of go through
items.example: Could we go through the contract before we sign it?
items.note: Go through a document, plan or set of belongings to inspect it carefully.

items.pt: ser aprovado; ser concluído com sucesso
items.section: C · Different meanings of go through
items.example: The proposed merger did not go through in the end.
items.note: Used for a deal, application or plan that is accepted or completed.

items.example: The frightened dog suddenly went for the cyclist.
items.note: In this meaning, go for someone suggests a sudden attack.

items.example: I think I'll go for the earlier train.
items.note: Go for a choice, option or candidate.

items.example: These dark shoes go with nearly every outfit I own.
items.note: Go with means look suitable together; especially clothes and colours.

items.pt: fazer dar certo; ter sucesso em
items.example: They worked hard to make a go of their new café.
items.note: Make a go of something means succeed in an undertaking despite difficulty.

items.pt: em atividade; ocupado o tempo todo
items.example: I've been on the go since six this morning.
items.note: Informal expression for being busy or continually active.

items.example: It goes without saying that safety comes first.
items.note: Introduces something considered obvious or understood.

items.pt: até certo ponto; dentro de seus limites
items.example: The report is useful as far as it goes, but it leaves out recent data.
items.note: Signals partial approval while noting that something is limited or incomplete.

items.example: The story goes that the building once housed a theatre.
items.note: Introduces a commonly repeated account that may not be verified.

items.pt: não medir esforços; fazer de tudo
items.example: The organisers went to great lengths to make the event accessible.
items.note: Usually followed by to + infinitive, expressing considerable effort.

items.example: Several small retailers went bankrupt during the recession.
items.note: Go plus adjective describes a change of state; bankrupt means unable to pay debts.

units.title: Unit 94 — Expressions with other common verbs
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 94. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Use frequent look, see, run, turn, let and break expressions accurately.
Distinguish literal and idiomatic meanings of common verb-based phrases.
Practise grammatical patterns, particles and register in original B2-level examples.

items.pt: aguardar com expectativa; ficar ansioso por
items.example: I look forward to hearing your feedback next week.
items.note: To is a preposition, so use a noun or -ing verb after it; common in correspondence.

items.example: The maintenance team is looking into the repeated failures.
items.note: Look into a problem or matter means investigate it.

items.example: Let's look at the evidence before we decide.
items.note: Here look at means consider or examine, not just see visually.

items.example: He looks down on colleagues who lack formal qualifications.
items.note: To consider someone inferior; the opposite attitude is look up to.

items.example: As a child, I looked up to my older sister.
items.note: Used for respect or admiration for another person.

items.example: The trip was cancelled, but let's look on the bright side: we can rest.
items.note: An expression encouraging optimism when circumstances are disappointing.

items.example: I'll see to the room bookings before the conference.
items.note: See to something means deal with it or make sure it is done.

items.pt: ver como resolver; cuidar de; providenciar
items.example: Could you see about organising transport for the guests?
items.note: See about something is common when arranging or finding a way to deal with it.

items.pt: despedir-se de alguém na partida; acompanhar até a saída
items.example: We went to the station to see our friends off.
items.note: See someone off means accompany them when they leave, e.g. at an airport or station.

items.example: She saw through the fake offer immediately.
items.note: See through someone or something means recognise the deception.

items.pt: estar vendo coisas; achar que está imaginando
items.example: I thought I was seeing things when I spotted a fox in the city centre.
items.note: Used when a sight is so unlikely that the speaker doubts their senses.

items.example: I ran into my former tutor at the supermarket.
items.note: Informal expression for an unexpected meeting.

items.example: Our patience ran out after another hour of waiting.
items.note: Intransitive: the supply, time or patience itself runs out.

items.pt: ficar sem; esgotar o estoque de
items.example: We've run out of printer paper again.
items.note: Transitive pattern: a person or group runs out of something.

items.example: Let's run over the main points before the presentation.
items.note: In this context, run over means review briefly, not drive over something.

items.example: Training new staff costs money now but saves time in the long run.
items.note: Refers to the eventual result over a long period.

items.example: The buses aren't running because of the heavy snow.
items.note: Used for vehicles and transport services operating on a schedule.

items.example: She turned down an attractive job offer.
items.note: Turn down an offer, invitation or request means refuse it.

items.example: Only half the invited guests turned up.
items.note: Informal for arrive or appear.

items.pt: mudar de comportamento; começar uma nova fase
items.example: He promised to turn over a new leaf and arrive on time.
items.note: Means make a fresh start by behaving better.

items.example: The simple repair turned out to be much more complicated.
items.note: Often used when the final reality differs from expectations.

items.example: I promised not to let the rest of the team down.
items.note: Let someone down means fail or disappoint them when they depend on you.

items.example: Don't let go of the handle until the gate is locked.
items.note: Let go of something means release your grip on it.

items.pt: liberar com punição leve; perdoar uma infração
items.example: The judge let the young offender off with a warning.
items.note: Often followed by with a warning or a fine; this is about lenient punishment.

items.pt: deixar escapar uma informação; revelar sem querer
items.example: She let it slip that the company was planning a merger.
items.note: Used when someone reveals confidential information, often accidentally.

items.example: He broke a promise to help his neighbours move.
items.note: Use break, not do, with a promise you fail to keep.

items.pt: interromper de repente; parar de falar
items.example: The speaker broke off when the alarm sounded.
items.note: In this context, someone suddenly stops speaking mid-sentence.

items.example: Nobody knew how to break the news to her.
items.note: Often means gently or carefully telling someone upsetting news.

items.example: It broke his heart to leave the place where he grew up.
items.note: Causing deep sadness, not a literal physical injury.

items.example: The cyclist hopes to break a national record this season.
items.note: Achieve a result better than the previous best; compare set a record.

items.example: Someone broke into the office during the weekend.
items.note: Break into a home or building means enter illegally, often by force; appears in the reflective exercise.
